newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU tries to reassure aspiring new members.
newsitem.headline: EU tries to reassure aspiring new members.

text.p: The European Union sought to reassure a queue of anxious aspirant countries on Friday that their ambitions to join the wealthy Western bloc would not fall victim to an internal EU power struggle.
But after a meeting between EU and the leaders of 12 eager applicant countries, many former Iron Curtain states remained none the wiser about when membership talks with them would start.
Briefing the 12 about its recent treaty-writing summit, the EU was at pains to stress all would be done to make sure the EU is ready to take in its new eastern members early next century.

The message was in contrast to the pessimistic tones by European Commission President Jacques Santer and Dutch Premier Wim Kok on Thursday, who told the European Parliament failure by the EU's June 16-17 summit to agree on institutional reforms augured badly for the EU expansion project.

"If these countries are ready to proceed I do not think, there will be a delay because of the EU, because that would be a slap in the face of these countries and their people," Kok told a news conference after the meeting.
"We have reassurances that these technical matters will not hold up enlargement, and for us this is the most important," Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati told reporters.
If easterners seemed reassured by the EU's words, they took their anxiety about who will negotiate entry and when back home with them.

"The discussions with the EU raised more questions than answers," Slovenian foreign minister Zoran Thaler told a news conference. "There was no answer to the question of with how many countries they will start the talks."
Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania and Bulgaria are all in the line.
The meeting took place as the eastern European countries nervously await the European Commission's assessment on July 16 of how suitable each of them is for the rigours of EU membership.
The EU has not yet decided whether to open talks with all or just some, and some fear it will limit the first expansion to five to make institutional adaptation easier.

Their angst is heightened by the fact that some of them face a double rejection as the NATO military alliance is expected to invite just three aspirants -- Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to its own first expansion at a July 8-9 summit, leaving out in the cold some countries trying hard to shake off their communist past.
"I think that if we get a sort-of double no to the EU and to NATO that would support Euroscepticism within these countries," Slovak Premier Vladimir Meciar warned at a news conference.
Commission President Jacques Santer said the EU executive would have different recommendations for each country.

"Even if they are based on objective criteria, most opinions will be different from country to country in that each country is different, some big, some less big... some have gone further with their structural reforms," he told the news conference.
Talks with Cyprus, which has already been judged to fit the bill, are due to start early next year.
Turkey's EU application has been shunned on human rights grounds and its presence on Friday signalled a renewed will on the part of the EU to make the secular state feel part of the European picture.

Kok stressed that while it was an applicant, it could not be considered a candidate for EU membership at the present time. "The status quo has not in any way changed following today's meeting," Kok said.
